title: Numbers and "have"
goal: Count, ask prices, and say you have something — in a language that has **no verb "to have"** at all.
bekal: count from zero up to a million without memorizing a hundred words
use *mul on* / *mul ei ole* to talk about possession
ask and understand prices in shops and markets

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Turul
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning at Balti jaam turg, the market by Tallinn's train station. Budi is shopping on his own for the first time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Hello! How much are the apples?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah. Kui palju maksab see leib?
lines.id: Yes. How much is this bread?
lines.literal: yes. how much costs-it this bread?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hea küll. Ja üks pudel vett.
lines.id: All right. And a bottle of water.
lines.literal: good enough. and one bottle water-PARTITIVE.

lines.speaker: Müüja:
lines.id: That's eight euros thirty cents in total.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vabandust, mul ei ole sularaha. Kas kaart sobib?
lines.id: Sorry, I don't have any cash. Is a card OK?
lines.literal: sorry, me-on not is cash-money. [question] card suits-it?

lines.speaker: Müüja:
lines.id: Of course. In Estonia everyone pays by card.

lines.speaker: Müüja:
lines.text: Isegi turul. Meil pole peaaegu üldse sularaha.
lines.id: Even at the market. We hardly have any cash at all.
lines.literal: even market-on. us-on not-is almost at-all cash-money.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Incredible. In Indonesia it's the opposite.

lines.speaker: Müüja:
lines.text: Palun, siin on tšekk. Head päeva!
lines.id: Here you go, here's your receipt. Have a good day!
lines.literal: please, here is receipt. good-GEN day-PARTITIVE!

notes: **Maksab** for one item, **maksavad** for several. Compare *maksab see leib* (one loaf) with *maksavad õunad* (many apples). Estonian verbs change with the number of the subject, just as English "costs" becomes "cost" — this gets full treatment in Unit 10.

⚠️ **Kaks euro*t*, kolmkümmend sen*ti*.** After a number, the noun takes the **partitive** form and **stays singular**. Not "kaks eurod". Your English instinct is right here — "two euros" is already plural in English, but Estonian keeps the noun singular and just changes its ending.
**Mul ei ole** and **meil pole** mean the same thing: "I/we don't have". *Pole* is short for *ei ole* and is very common in conversation. Use either; both are correct.
**Kaardiga** = *kaart* + **-ga** ("with"). The same ending works for payment methods, tools, and vehicles: *sularahaga* (with cash), *bussiga* (by bus), *pastakaga* (with a pen).

grammars.title: Numbers — and two secrets that cut the memorizing
body: You don't need to memorize a hundred words. Estonian builds all its numbers from ten basic words and two patterns.
after: **Secret one: -teist.** The numbers 11–19 are the digit + *-teist*, meaning "from the second ten". *Üksteist* is literally "one of the second ten" = 11. Once you know 1–10, you know 11–19 with no extra memorizing — much like English "-teen".

**Secret two: 8 and 9 are subtractions.** *Kaheksa* contains *kaks* (two), *üheksa* contains *üks* (one) — they mean "two less than ten" and "one less than ten". Latin used the same trick (*undeviginti* = 19, "one from twenty"). Once you see it, the two words stop feeling random.

**Tens:** the digit + *-kümmend*. For the numbers in between, just add the unit on the end: *kakskümmend üks* (21), *nelikümmend seitse* (47), *üheksakümmend üheksa* (99). The order is the same as in English: tens first, then ones.

grammars.title: ⚠️ "Have" — without a verb "to have"
body: Estonian has no equivalent of "to have". It builds the idea another way: **"at me is X"**.
after: The forms *mul, sul, tal, meil, teil, neil* are the pronoun + the ending **-l**, the same ending as in *Saksamaal* in Unit 2. So you're not learning six new words — you're seeing an old ending do a new job.

**Making it negative:** *mul ei ole* or *mul pole*. *Mul pole autot.* (I don't have a car.) ⚠️ Note that after a negative, the thing owned goes into the **partitive**: *auto* → *autot*. That rule is covered in Units 11 and 13; for now just know that the ending changes.
**Asking:** *Kas sul on...?* — *Kas sul on aega?* (Do you have time?), *Kas teil on kohvi?* (Do you have coffee?). You'll use that second sentence every day in cafés and shops.

blocks.title: Saying prices like an Estonian
items: Full price: *kolm eurot viiskümmend senti* — three euros fifty cents.
In daily speech people shorten it: *kolm viiskümmend*, just like English "three fifty".
⚠️ The decimal comma is read *koma*: *3,50* = *kolm koma viis*. And the decimal mark really is a **comma**, not a point — so *3,50* is "3.50" in English notation.

⚠️ *odav* means cheap, *kallis* means expensive — but *kallis* also means "dear" when addressing someone. *Kallis Kerli!* at the start of a letter means "Dear Kerli", not "Expensive Kerli" — the same double life as English "dear".

blocks.text: ⚠️ Phone numbers in Estonia are read **digit by digit**, not grouped into pairs or chunks the way some English speakers do ("twenty-five, forty-three"). If you dictate a number, slow down and say each digit separately.

blocks.title: Ordinal numbers — when you need them
items: Used for floors (*teine korrus*), dates (*kolmas mai*), and order (*esimene kord* — the first time).
⚠️ *Esimene* and *teine* follow no pattern — memorize them (like "first" and "second" in English). The rest are fairly regular: the cardinal number + *-s*.

Fill in the correct form of mul on or mul ei ole.
Put the words in the right order.
